title: grep and Regular Expressions
subtitle: Searching file content with grep, egrep, and basic regex patterns
author: KERNAL Team

content.code:
# Basic: search for a pattern in a file
grep "ERROR" server.log            # lines containing ERROR
grep "error" server.log            # case-sensitive
grep -i "error" server.log         # -i: case-insensitive
grep -n "ERROR" server.log         # -n: show line numbers
grep -c "ERROR" server.log         # -c: count matching lines
grep -v "DEBUG" server.log         # -v: invert (lines NOT matching)
grep -l "TODO" *.js                # -l: only print filenames

# Search recursively in a directory
grep -r "console.log" ./src/       # -r: recursive
grep -rn "TODO" ./src/             # with line numbers
grep -ri "password" ./config/      # recursive + case-insensitive

# Context lines
grep -A 3 "ERROR" server.log       # 3 lines After match
grep -B 2 "ERROR" server.log       # 2 lines Before match
grep -C 5 "ERROR" server.log       # 5 lines Context (before + after)

# Exact word match
grep -w "log" server.log           # 'log' not 'logging' or 'changelog'

# . matches any single character
grep "e.g" file.txt     # matches 'egg', 'e-g', 'e g'

# ^ matches start of line, $ matches end of line
grep "^Error" file.txt  # lines starting with 'Error'
grep "done$" file.txt   # lines ending with 'done'
grep "^$" file.txt      # empty lines

# * matches zero or more of the preceding char
grep "colou*r" file.txt # matches 'color', 'colour', 'colouur'

# [] matches any character in the set
grep "[0-9]" file.txt   # lines with at least one digit
grep "[A-Z]" file.txt   # lines with uppercase letters
grep "[^a-z]" file.txt  # lines with non-lowercase chars

# Extended regex with -E (or use egrep)
grep -E "error|warning|fatal" server.log   # OR
grep -E "^[0-9]{4}-" timestamps.txt        # starts with 4 digits + dash
grep -E "https?://" urls.txt              # http or https
grep -E "\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,}\b" text.txt  # email

content.text: Use grep -E for extended regex (alternation |, +, ?, {n}) and grep -P for Perl-compatible regex (\d, \w, \s). Quote your patterns in single quotes to prevent the shell from interpreting special characters.

questions.question: You want to find all lines in access.log that do NOT contain '200' (success responses). Which command?
questions.explanation: grep -v (invert match) prints lines that do NOT match the pattern. grep -v '200' access.log shows all lines where '200' does not appear — useful for finding error responses (4xx, 5xx) in web server logs.

faq.q: What is the difference between grep, egrep, and fgrep?
faq.a: grep uses basic regex. egrep (same as grep -E) uses extended regex with |, +, ?, {}. fgrep (same as grep -F) treats the pattern as a literal string (no regex) — faster when searching for fixed strings like file paths or error codes. In modern scripts, prefer grep -E and grep -F flags over the egrep/fgrep aliases.

examples: grep -rn 'process.env' ./src | grep -v '.test.' — find all env var usages in source, excluding test files
grep -E '"status":\s*[45][0-9]{2}' api.log — find all 4xx/5xx responses in a JSON API log
